newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia opposition says protests will continue.
newsitem.headline: Serbia opposition says protests will continue.

text.p: Serbia's opposition said on Friday it was not satisfied with the Socialist government's partial acknowledgement of its victory in November elections and declared it would continue street protests.

A letter from Yugoslav foreign minister Milan Milutinovic to the Organisation of Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) acknowledged the opposition won nine municipalities in Belgrade in local elections.
But Milutinovic did not acknowledge the opposition won in other big towns and added the authorities still needed more detail to clarify results in some places.
Vuk Draskovic, one of the leaders of the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition, described Milutinovic's letter as a smokescreen that effectively spurned OSCE recommendations.

"Lies, lies, lies. This is typical of (Serbian President Slobodan) Milosevic -- using tricks to (outwit) the international community...We reject this shameful letter of lies and manipulations," he told Reuters.

Zajedno, backed by thousands of students, launched mass protests for 47 days running after the ruling Socialists (SPS) annulled poll results that gave the opposition victory in 15 of Serbia's 18 largest towns, including Belgrade.
Milutinovic's letter was a response to an OSCE report by former Spanish prime minister Felipe Gonzalez who led a mission to Serbia to investigate the disputed elections.
The OSCE, invited by Milosevic in a bid to defuse opposition protests and international criticism, acknowledged Zajedno victories in the 15 cities.

"Milutinovic's reply makes patently clear that Milosevic not only rejects... the OSCE's recommendations, but also deliberately misleads the world about the election results in Serbia," Zajedno's legal department said in a statement.
Milutinovic declared the Zajedno coalition has formed a municipal assembly in Zrenjanin, which was a lie, it said.

"The SPS (Socialists) have prevented these legally-elected local officials from assuming their duties, because of which Zajedno's deputies have for several days been staging a protest inside the municipal assembly building," it said.
Zajedno also disputed Milutinovic's assertion about results in several provincial towns.

"In all these towns, Zajedno won absolute majorities at votes held on November 17 -- but by forging election results in competent commissions and by way of subsequent illegal decisions of courts, which are completely controlled by the regime, the SPS annulled Zajedno's victories," it said.

In the case of Nis, "where Zajedno's victory is beyond any doubt" a municipal electoral commission made up exclusively of SPS members continues to forge election records and vote counts despite a court order awarding the opposition victory, it said.
In Belgrade, where the opposition won the city assembly and eleven municipalities Zajedno has been able to form local authorities in only five areas, the statement said.
There was no mention about the Belgrade city assembly where Zajedno won a convincing majority, it said.
"It has become very clear that Milosevic has opted for a conflict with the whole world in an effort to stay in power."
Zoran Djindjic, a Zajedno leader who would have been Belgrade mayor if the socialists had handed over power, said he was confident Milosevic would succumb in time.
"They (socialists) will return the votes to us in ten or fifteen days, when the world puts pressure on them - but our main problem remains that they will remain the thieves that they are," he said.

Milan Bozic, Draskovic's policy advisor, said the regime was just buying time. "But in the long run I am very optimistic because this shows that the regime has definitely started crumbling from within."
